---
title: "4.1 Forces on curved surfaces"
---

{{< include ../_checkpoint-widget.qmd >}}

## The big idea

We will continue to use surface integrals to calculate the net force due to pressure on a surface (and we'll continue to do so with moving fluids in the next unit). It takes a lot of Calculus III to do this when the surface is curved! The surface normal is not constant, meaning the local force per area (~pressure) points in different directions; pressure is simply a function of depth but we'll need to write it in terms of a radial coordinate; then, I guess we'll need to integrate in terms of radius?

This is often considered the toughest section in the course!

## Think first

**Recall**

1. Surface normals are vectors, and the force due to pressure acts normal to surfaces.
2. From the last reading: we integrate pressure over area to get force, and need to write $dA$ in terms of the coordinates in the problems.

**Look ahead**

1. What is the difference between the $x$ coordinate and the $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ unit vector?
2. We built-up a double integral for finding force on a plane... how can we do the same when the surface is curved?

## Coordinates vs. directions

One concept we need to understand in multivariable calculus is this: a **coordinate** is not the same as a **direction**. In Cartesian, $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$, $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$, and $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ always point in the same directions and they always have magnitude 1 (they are unit vectors). The coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can vary — they can assume positive or negative values, or be zero. They can go to infinity.

There is a small hiccup in cylindrical coordinates: $\hat{\mathbf{r}}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{\theta}}$ actually change their orientation in physical space, depending on location. This is why conservation of momentum in the $\hat{\mathbf{r}}$- and $\hat{\mathbf{\theta}}$-directions is really tough (though we will see how to deal with it when we look at the Navier-Stokes Equations). But, let's recognize that these unit vectors also have magnitude 1 and, at least at a given location, they always point in the same directions (radial is away from the origin, angular is along a path where we get no closer to the origin). And coordinates $(r,\theta,z)$ can assume any values (with the caveats that $r\geq 0$ and $\theta$ is only useful from $0\rightarrow 2\pi$).


::: {.callout-important}
The unit vectors of the coordinate system are always **orthogonal**, meaning that, if you dot any two of them together in a given coordinate system, that dot product is zero. $\hat{\mathbf{x}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{z}}=0$. $\hat{\mathbf{r}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{\theta}}=0$. $\hat{\mathbf{r}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{z}}=0$. $\hat{\mathbf{z}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{\theta}}=0$. Dotting $\hat{\mathbf{x}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{\theta}}$ is a more complicated result, but we try to avoid blending coordinate system directions.
:::

However, there are occasions when it makes sense to mix Cartesian directions with cylindrical or spherical coordinates. The surface of a spherical ball is most easily described in terms of $(r,\theta,\phi)$ coordinates, but if we were interested in the buoyancy of the ball, that would be a force in the $-\hat{\mathbf{y}}$-direction (depending on how you define the coordinates). So, calculating the force on a ball, it would make sense to integrate over $(r=R=\text{constant},\theta,\phi)$, but to prepare the equation in such a way that you return the force in the $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$-direction. That is: **we'd need to figure out how to write the pressure in terms of $\theta$ and $\phi$**, and **somehow just a vertical component would emerge**.


## Set-up as an integral
Pressure is a scalar **field** quantity, meaning we can evaluate its value at any location in space and time: $p(\mathbf{x},t)$. When it comes to evaluating forces due to pressure, we would need to consider the values of pressure at the surface location, and we would also need to consider the orientation of the surface. Surfaces are 2D objects, meaning, in general, two coordinates will need to vary to completely describe a surface. The geometry of the situation will imply what coordinates are easiest to use.

::: {.column-margin}
We'll use $p(\mathbf{x},t)$ generically, with $\mathbf{x}$ a vector of coordinates in any coordinate system.
:::

A general statement of the above is

$$
    \mathbf{F}=\int\limits_S -p(\mathbf{x})\hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{x})dA.
$$

Describing it in detail: Within the integrand we have $-p(\mathbf{x})\hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{x})$. This is a quantity that describes the magnitude of the pressure at a given location, as well as the local surface orientation (which may depend on the coordinate). By multiplying these two variables together, we get the local force-per-area due to pressure. We need to sum the force-per-area, keeping in mind that it is a vector, over the entire surface area to get the total force.

::: {.column-margin}
We're using the convention that the surface normal points from the surface, into the fluid, hence $\mathbf{F} \sim - \hat{\mathbf{n}}$.
:::

### Task 1: Determine the coordinates to integrate over, and the bounds
We must decide what coordinates to integrate over — namely, what coordinates describe the location on the surface. For a flat object, it usually makes sense to use Cartesian coordinates, though we might rotate these coordinates to make our bounds a bit easier to describe — see [Angled surfaces](../unit-3/p-int.qmd#angled-surfaces) from the last reading.

In cylindrical coordinates, there are two basic surfaces: the circular "cap" and the curved wall. For the circle, $r$ and $\theta$ vary over the surface, and so we will be integrating with respect to $dA = r dr d\theta$.

::: {.column-margin}
Where did I get $dA = r dr d\theta$ from? Notice that $dA = dr d\theta$ is not a dimensionally consistent equation!
:::

::: {.callout-important}
Though we might be integrating with respect to $r$ and $\theta$, we might still have that our integrand depends on $z$! So what should we do!?

Assuming we've defined everything reasonably, we should have that $z$ is a constant on this surface. A very basic example: the bottom of a cylindrical pool, with a circular bottom. We'd use $p=\rho g z$ and have $z=H=\text{constant}$.
:::

```{=html}
<div class="fl-checkpoint"
     data-prompt="Integrating over an entire circle — what's the lower bound on θ?"
     data-answer="0" data-tol="0.02" data-units="rad"
     data-hint="A circle has no natural starting angle, so we're free to pick the convenient one."
     data-solution="θ: 0 → ⋯ — we start wherever's convenient, and 0 is the convenient choice."
     data-target="ci-theta-upper"></div>
```

::: {#ci-theta-upper .fl-hidden}
Going all the way around covers the full angle, so the upper bound is some multiple of $\pi$:

```{=html}
<div class="fl-checkpoint"
     data-prompt="Upper bound is nπ — what is n?"
     data-answer="2" data-tol="0.02" data-units=""
     data-hint="A full circle is 360°. How many π-radians is that?"
     data-solution="θ: 0 → 2π — one full trip around the circle covers 2π radians (360°)."></div>
```
:::

For a different problem in which we need to evaluate the force on the curved part of the cylinder: $\theta$ and $z$ vary over the surface. So we'd write $dA=Rd\theta dz$ (where the radius still needs to be included, though now it is a constant $r=R$). And maybe we integrate $z:0\rightarrow L$, the length of the cylinder, and $\theta:0\rightarrow 2\pi$. (Again, depends on the specifics of the geometry, but I'm just giving some examples without putting in the effort of including a picture!)

### Task 2: Determine the corresponding normal vector
Once we have settled on the coordinates used in $dA$, this tells us the **coordinates** for both $p$ and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ (so that we can complete the integration). However, we may consider writing the **direction** of $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ in other systems, e.g. in Cartesian such that we can get the buoyant or lift force in $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ or the drag force in $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$. To emphasize: we may write $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ in terms of $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$-, $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$-, and $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$-components, but those components may be written in cylindrical **coordinates**.

We need to lean on trigonometry to figure these things out. A quick example: for a fluid surrounding a circle centered on the origin, the normal direction always acts radially outward: $\hat{\mathbf{n}}=\hat{\mathbf{r}}$. We can represent this in terms of cylindrical components:

$$
\hat{\mathbf{n}}=\left<n_r,n_\theta,n_z\right>=
\left<1,0,0\right>
$$
but maybe we would like to know the lift and drag forces. Assuming the usual coordinate systems, we can instead write
$$
    \hat{\mathbf{n}}=\left<n_x,n_y,n_z\right>=
    \left<\cos\theta,\sin\theta,0\right>.
$$

This complicates the integrand, a bit, but we will have no problems with computing it with a tool like Wolfram Alpha.


::: {.callout-note}
We recognize that the integrand now has **components**, which may be a bit scary! No problem: in general, we can just divide the integral up into components and do basic integration on each component.
:::


### Task 3: Determine the pressure distribution in our chosen coordinates
We must also write $p(\mathbf{x})$ in terms of the coordinates we are integrating over. For hydrostatics, the typical starting point is

$$
p(y)=\rho g y
$$

where $y=0$ at the free surface (so we are dealing with gauge pressure) and we have flexibility in choosing whether $y$ increases or decreases with depth. Here let's say that $y>0$ below the surface.

We are technically only interested in the pressure distribution **on the surface**, and so need to write the pressure as a function of the variables on the surface. This is very situation-dependent, but here is a quick example: For the circle described in the previous section, the center of the circle is located at a depth $H$, and the circle has radius $R<H$. Focusing on the coordinate system defined from the circles' center, we would like to write the pressure as a function of $\theta$ since that varies at the surface. It will also depend on $R$, but will **not** be a function of $r$, because $r$ is not varying on the surface. And I guess this "circle" should be thought of as a cylinder with coordinate $z$ extending into the page — for this configuration, pressure does not depend on $z$, but we would be integrating with respect to $z$.

I am purposely being a bit vague and incomplete so that we can still write a homework problem about this!
